props.title: Bruce Almighty
props.initialSlug: A man is given God's powers to learn about responsibility

sections.content: Bruce Almighty (2003) stands as Jim Carrey's perfect blend of his signature physical comedy and genuine emotional depth. The film tackles existential questions about faith, free will, and human responsibility through the lens of comedy, similar to how Groundhog Day (1993) used its supernatural premise to explore personal growth. Director Tom Shadyac, who previously worked with Carrey on Ace Ventura: Pet Detective (1994) and Liar Liar (1997), strikes a delicate balance between broad humor and spiritual contemplation.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of divine intervention comedies in the 2000s. Click (2006) borrowed the "supernatural power with consequences" template, while Evan Almighty (2007) attempted to expand the universe with diminishing returns. Morgan Freeman's portrayal of God became instantly iconic, joining George Burns in Oh, God! (1977) and Alanis Morissette in Dogma (1999) as memorable divine screen presences.

The visual effects, while dated by today's standards, serve the story's comedic elements perfectly. Scenes like Bruce lassoing the moon and parting his soup like the Red Sea demonstrate how CGI can enhance rather than overshadow comedy. This approach influenced later supernatural comedies like The Mask (1994) and Bedtime Stories (2008). SUBHEAD: Impact on Religious-Themed Comedy

sections.content: Bruce Almighty proved that mainstream comedies could tackle religious themes without alienating audiences. The film paved the way for movies like Year One (2009) and This Is The End (2013), which mixed religious imagery with contemporary humor. It's particularly noteworthy how the film manages to be reverent while remaining genuinely funny, avoiding the heavy-handedness of traditional faith-based films.
